summary: This paper demonstrates quantum simulation of two- and three-flavor neutrino oscillations using Fock-basis encoding of a microwave cavity mode in superconducting circuits, with control via SNAP and displacement gates applied to an ancillary transmon qubit. Pulse-level simulations show oscillation probabilities in close agreement with theoretical predictions despite gate fidelities reduced to ~0.97 (two-flavor) and ~0.925 (three-flavor) by ancilla decoherence.
motivation: Cavity bosonic encodings offer advantages over qubit-based approaches including long coherence times (~1 ms for 3D cavities) and reduced control hardware complexity, making them attractive for quantum simulation of particle physics phenomena.
method: Arbitrary unitary operations on the cavity Fock subspace are implemented by interleaving sequences of displacement operations $D(\alpha)$ (Gaussian pulses on cavity drive) and SNAP gates $S(\vec{\theta})$ (conditional number-dependent ancilla rotations via flat-top Gaussian pulses lasting ~2.77 µs). Two-flavor oscillations use direct compilation; three-flavor oscillations use optimized sequences of building blocks $B(\alpha, \vec{\theta}) = D^\dagger(\alpha) S(\vec{\theta}) D(\alpha)$ with gradient-descent parameter optimization via JAX.
result: Direct-compilation fidelities reached $>0.99$ for two-flavor and $\approx 0.99$ for three-flavor protocols; pulse-level simulations with $T_1 = 100$ µs and $T_\phi \approx 55$ µs yielded fidelities of $\approx 0.97$ and $\approx 0.925$ respectively, with simulated neutrino oscillation probabilities matching theory across the full range of $L/E$ values tested.
